pr_title: drivers: flash: sam0: Resolve write issues in the first row
pr_body:
Previously, while writing close to the start of flash (i.e: in the first row), the write was never committed - due to zero being used as the "empty buffer" marker.

This patch also incorporates some performance improvements, as well as observing any errors reported by `flash_sam0_commit()`.

Fixes #52309
Supersedes #51976
pr_comments: @attie-argentum, you can forget about my remark over `len ==0`, it is exactly at the right place in code.
@nandojve can you please take a look?

issue_context.title: SAM0 flash driver with page emulated enabled will not write data at 0 block
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
I tried to port my program which updates bootloader from main program.
I discovered that program will not update in first page (for example offset 0-128)

Updates doesn't happen because code assumes that nobody will not write any data in first flash page.

**To Reproduce**
1. Use any SAM0 board for example C21N Xpro
2. Make program which changes flash in first page - for example 0 offset
3. Discover that nothing changes in flash

**Expected behavior**
Flash operation should work for all block/page even in 0 offset.

**Impact**
Flash driver

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - Any SAM0 board
comments:
@benys, would it not be better to initialize (and reset) the offset to an invalid value of the flash_size ?

Please also realize that this BYTE_EMULATION is prone to errors as a result of power failure. When the power is cut just after the erase there will be no data in flash. Using this as a way to provide support for e.g. mcuboot could result in a non-recoverable error.

@Laczen I thought about initialize with flash_size but I am pretty new in project and I don't know that DEFINE exists for that. I will try find.

Good point, Yes I know it, but honestly I found this problem when I ported flash driver to handle flash RWW space. At some SAM0 RWW space is small flash space which is dedicated to store some persistent variables.

@benys , you can find it as `CONFIG_FLASH_SIZE * 1024`, see

https://github.com/benys/zephyr/blob/3262783360c3f28a8054406e01c9257359562e32/drivers/flash/flash_sam0.c#L61

review_comments:
The `len == 0` check should not be required and gracefully handled by the writing routine. These checks are polluting the code and are a bad idea:
1. Trying to return quickly on a condition that should not appear is adding a comparison to all real writes,
2. Handling the write of `len == 0` as a normal write could enable detection that there is something wrong with the interface without doing a real write.

I'd suggest that this _is_ the "_graceful_" handling of a zero-length write...

> Trying to return quickly on a condition that should not appear is adding a comparison to all real writes,

Its impact is incredibly minimal... but if others agree, I'll remove it.
I think the sensible alternative to an early return is for **_two_** guards - one around each `flash_sam0_write_protection()`.

> Handling the write of `len == 0` as a normal write could enable detection that there is something wrong with the interface without doing a real write.

You can't get much closer to the lower level calls than this - `flash_sam0_commit()` won't be called with `len == 0` anyway... and as above, it would be sensible to add more guards.

@attie-argentum, what I mean by graceful handling is that whatever follows is not influenced by this check (and I think it is already handled, nothing will happen if the line is removed). There shouldn't be an "early return", why should there be, it is no error condition.

An extra guard is also not required, if the flash_sam0_write_protection would fail for a write of 0 this is interesting knowledge that could be usefull. It would allow using a write of zero length to verify if it can write. The same holds for trying to write outside of the region, it will return an error message.

I'm not going to argue the point too hard - I'll remove the check if needs be...

I suppose I prefer to protect the hardware from bad users - i.e: the unnecessary "_unprotect_" → "_re-protect_" process that is incurred by a zero-length write, which would be detrimental to the device's lifespan if it's over-used...

If you're trying to write, why not just try to write? A zero-length write only checks that the start is in-range, not the whole target region, so it's of limited use (but `flash_sam0_valid_range()` is still called in this case).

The docs don't mention anything about zero-length writes ([link](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/3.2.0/hardware/peripherals/flash.html#c.flash_write)), and in this mode (with `SOC_FLASH_SAM0_EMULATE_BYTE_PAGES` defined), we're already doing a lot of hand-holding for the user...

In fact, other drivers implement this check too! 🙃

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/e5efa3dfffd8d3eba0ae4bb580c535dadacfc7f9/drivers/flash/flash_sam.c#L180-L182

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/e5efa3dfffd8d3eba0ae4bb580c535dadacfc7f9/drivers/flash/flash_stm32.c#L220-L222

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/e5efa3dfffd8d3eba0ae4bb580c535dadacfc7f9/drivers/flash/flash_gd32.c#L58-L60

> I'm not going to argue the point too hard - I'll remove the check if needs be...
> 

Neither am I. 😀 

> I suppose I prefer to protect the hardware from bad users - i.e: the unnecessary "_unprotect_" → "_re-protect_" process that is incurred by a zero-length write, which would be detrimental to the device's lifespan if it's over-used...
>

That is a good reason, and should be the only reason to do this.
 
> In fact, other drives implement this check too! 🙃

I know, but this shouldn't stop you from trying to do better. 😀

> but this shouldn't stop you from trying to do better

Now there's a controversial statement... I thought I _was_ trying to do better 😜

... I'll let others chip in on the `len == 0` test, I hope that's okay.

The `len == 0` checks area quite common in the flash code for write/read/erase ops.
In well tested code they are probably not needed, to guard user from mistakes, and if somebody relays on functions returning 0 when `len == 0`, that is happening because the person does have internal knowledge of flash driver source or gets that from experimenting with API (which is bad anyway).
Behaviour when `len == 0` is not explicitly documented in API.

I am actually curious why this is the second check after range, as `len == 0` may expect no work to happen, so why fail on incorrect range when range is not going to be used anyway? 
In GD32 flash the erase bails out with 0 when `len == 0`, before checking range.

Btw. There is `CHECIF` maro that evaluates only when `CONFIG_NO_RUNTIME_CHECKS` is enabled, and it is often used to enable/disable NULL checks in various places.
